articles.title: Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear
articles.author: Monique Mitchell Turner, Professor of Communication, Michigan State University
paras: On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers watched a little girl counting petals on a flower. Her voice gave way to a man counting down, and then a nuclear blast filled the screen.

The ad ran as a paid spot only once, in support of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s reelection campaign. It never mentioned his opponent, republican Barry Goldwater. The ad played on a fear voters already held, that Goldwater might start a nuclear war. Republicans protested loudly, Democrats pulled the spot, and the uproar got it rebroadcast in full on network news.

I study how emotional appeals persuade, from how viewers’ moods shape their reactions to political ads to how anxiety drives people to seek out, and sometimes fail to absorb, information about threats.
The LBJ “Daisy” ad shows why political campaigns to this day continue to reach for fear, and it hints at why the payoff is less predictable than you might think.
Fear is an alarm. It tells you something threatening is close. You feel scared when you believe you are at risk from something dangerous that can hurt you.
Anxiety knocks people off autopilot, sharpens attention and sends them looking for new information. That heightened attentiveness may be exactly what a struggling campaign wants.

When political scientists Travis Ridout and Kathleen Searles tracked Senate ads from 2004, they found that front-runners often leaned on enthusiasm and pride in their messaging, while candidates who were behind leaned on fear and anger.

During the 1998 Massachusetts governor’s race, political scientist Ted Brader ran a study that embedded campaign ads in a news broadcast and changed only the music and images, keeping the words identical. Those changes produced completely different reactions. When a negative ad paired grainy black-and-white images of drug use with tense music, viewers paid closer attention to the spoken message and became more open to reconsidering their chosen candidate.

Fear cues – like a nuclear mushroom cloud – can push viewers to weigh fresh information and reconsider their choice. One surprise: Politically informed citizens were more responsive to these emotional cues than less engaged ones. Fear is not simply a tool for swaying the uninformed, undecided voter. It also reaches people who follow politics closely. Emotion provides the motivation, while knowledge provides the ability to think carefully about the issues and positions and seek out more information.

More broadly, a meta-analysis of over 100 studies found that fear appeals reliably shift attitudes and behavior across health and other domains. For instance, public health researcher Lucy Popova tested fear-based messages designed to discourage smokers from trying snus, a smokeless tobacco product. She found that when participants perceived a serious threat but also felt capable of acting on it, they held less favorable attitudes toward snus and were less inclined to try it.

Political attack ads – fear messaging being one type – have a shakier record. A review of more than 100 studies found no dependable evidence that negative campaigning wins elections, and some evidence that it lowers positive feelings toward the candidate who sponsors it.
The critical ingredient is empowerment

Communication scholar Kim Witte’s research found that fear motivates action when people believe there is a workable response that they can carry out. When the threat feels big and the solution feels out of reach, people protect themselves from the message instead. They tune out, deny the threat or decide the messenger is the problem.

For example, picture an ad geared toward adolescent vaping that shows teens in hospital beds with ventilators using scary terms like “popcorn lungs.” If the ad also communicates that vaping can destroy lungs irreversibly, the teen audience is likely to experience extreme fear while at the same time feeling like there’s no way to fix the problem.

My colleagues and I have seen this effect in our own experiments. We found that people who felt highly anxious and also confident they could act sought out the most information. Those who felt anxious but lacked that confidence did go looking, yet they recalled very little. Anxiety pushed them to search but got in the way of absorbing what they read.
A campaign that frightens voters without offering a clear step to address the issue could end up producing plenty of anxious attention and very little learning.

Empowerment also helps explain who shows up at the polls. Political scientist Nicholas Valentino and colleagues found that anger boosted voter participation more reliably than anxiety, and anxiety mattered mainly for people who already had the skills and resources to take actions like donate to campaigns, attend rallies, sign petitions and so on.
Fear plays on prejudice and stereotypes
Fear does its most reliable work when it attaches to a stereotype voters already carry. The 1988 presidential race provides two classic examples.

One controversial ad, produced in support of Republican George H.W. Bush, showed a mugshot of a Black man. The ad named the man, Willie Horton, and a voiceover explained that he’d committed rape and assault while on a weekend furlough from prison as part of a program run under Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis, the Democratic candidate. The spot linked fears about crime to race without saying so directly.

Bush’s campaign followed up with the “Revolving Door” ad, which built on that anxiety. It featured stark, black-and-white footage of inmates marching through a revolving gate while a narrator warned that Dukakis had let murderers out of prison on weekend passes.

Political scientist Tali Mendelberg’s research described in “The Race Card” shows that these implicit appeals to prejudices and fears are powerful. But they lose much of their force once someone publicly names them as racial. Implicit appeals work because they slip past most voters’ commitment to racial equality; once the racial message is pointed out, voters recognize it and many reject it rather than see themselves as endorsing prejudice.
Gender works in a similar way.

In a national experiment, Public Policy researcher Mirya Holman and colleagues found that when campaign messages triggered fears of terrorism, voters turned to their stereotypes of strong leaders as masculine. Those stereotypes hurt a female Democratic candidate, while Republican candidates of either gender were unaffected, since Republicans are already seen as tough on security.

A message communicating a threat does not need to name a candidate’s identity to disadvantage them. It simply makes voters reach for the stereotypes they already hold. There’s less systematic research on candidates’ religion, though the same mechanism – fear pushing voters to rely on the stereotypes they already hold about who can keep them safe – predicts similar vulnerability for Muslim candidates.
Is fear a more common tactic now?
Using fear as a campaign tool is nothing new.

In 1828, opponents accused presidential candidate Andrew Jackson of murder and cannibalism. Both parties have leaned on fear in the television era, from Reagan’s 1984 “Bear” ad about an unnamed Soviet threat, to Democrats’ 1996 warnings that seniors’ Medicare was at risk.

What has grown is negativity overall. Political scientist John Geer’s analysis of presidential ads from 1960 to 2004 documents that rise, though he also found attack ads, more likely than positive ones, to focus on real issues rather than personal traits. The evidence that fear specifically has increased, as opposed to negativity in general, is less clear.

The current media landscape shifts this dynamic significantly; while traditional nightly news broadcasts have seen a decline in viewership, targeted social media feeds have become the emotional battleground.

Recent digital campaign data shows that negative ads are highly prized online because they successfully grab attention by provoking strong emotions like fear and anger. Because platform recommendation systems are heavily driven by user activity, campaigns are incentivized to use emotionally charged appeals to maximize viral engagement across feeds.

Fear works less like a switch and more like a spotlight. It grabs attention and opens minds to change, but whether that turns into a vote, a boycott of the ballot box or resentment toward the messenger depends on what comes next.

articles.title: For Andy Burnham, getting closer to the EU could prove as tricky as exiting it – an expert explains
articles.author: Monika Brusenbauch Meislová, Visiting Professor, School of Law and Social Sciences, Aston University
paras: Andy Burnham has reopened a debate that successive UK prime ministers tried to settle. But the history of Brexit suggests that getting closer to the European Union may prove just as difficult as leaving it.

For years, prime ministers have attempted to put Brexit behind them. Burnham has just done the opposite. By suggesting that Britain could “go all the way” and rejoin the EU, he has broken with the cautious approach of his predecessors.
His intervention has brought renewed urgency to the question: how close should Britain remain to the EU, and on what terms?

The options are not new. From Theresa May’s attempts to secure a bespoke deal to Boris Johnson’s hard Brexit, Rishi Sunak’s pragmatism and Keir Starmer’s reset, governments have grappled with essentially the same dilemma. That is, how can the country retain the benefits of cooperation with the EU without accepting the obligations that come with it?
May: trying to have it both ways

Theresa May entered Downing Street with the task of delivering Brexit but no blueprint for doing so. Her declaration that “Brexit means Brexit” concealed a fundamental contradiction: she promised to leave the single market and customs union, end free movement and end the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice in Britain. But she also vowed to preserve close economic ties with the bloc.

May’s hopes for a bespoke deal clashed with the EU’s insistence that market access came with obligations. Her compromises satisfied neither hardline Brexit supporters nor pro-European MPs, ultimately bringing down her premiership. May’s experience exposed a dilemma that would haunt her successors. The closer Britain sought to remain to the EU, the harder it became to deliver the “control” promised by Brexit.
Johnson: getting Brexit done, but not settled

Boris Johnson offered a seemingly straightforward solution: stop searching for a compromise and embrace a more distant relationship. His promise to “get Brexit done” helped to secure a decisive election victory in 2019. Britain formally left the EU in January 2020, followed by an agreement that preserved tariff-free trade in qualifying goods but introduced new barriers such as customs checks and additional paperwork.

Yet withdrawal did not resolve the relationship. Trading frictions and disputes over Northern Ireland kept Brexit politically alive, exposing a paradox: delivering Brexit threatened to deprive its supporters of the very issue that had mobilised them. In other words, for politicians who had built their appeal around Brexit, declaring the job done risked losing a powerful means of rallying voters. The search for new Brexit victories therefore continued long after Britain had left.
Sunak: pragmatism without rapprochement

Rishi Sunak inherited a relationship marked by confrontation and mistrust. His approach was more pragmatic. The Windsor Framework of 2023 eased tensions that surrounded Northern Ireland’s post-Brexit trading arrangements, helping to restore trust between London and Brussels.

He also secured Britain’s association with Horizon Europe, an EU funding programme for research and innovation. These were significant practical achievements, but they did not amount to a fundamental rethink on Brexit. Sunak continued to champion the opportunities of regulatory independence while seeking to repair some of the disruption caused by withdrawal.
Starmer: the limits of the reset

Keir Starmer went further, promising to reset relations with the EU after years of confrontation from Conservative PMs. The Labour government pursued closer cooperation on security, trade and regulatory matters, but retained three crucial red lines: no return to the single market, no customs union and no freedom of movement.

This created a familiar problem. Britain wanted closer economic integration while continuing to reject some of the institutional arrangements that made it possible. The controversy surrounding a proposed youth mobility scheme underlined the political sensitivities involved in even limited steps towards closer ties. The reset offered opportunities for practical improvements, but its incremental approach could not eliminate the fundamental trade-offs of being outside the EU.
Burnham: a different route or the same dilemma?

Burnham now has two broad routes. The first is to deepen cooperation without pursuing full membership. A customs union could reduce barriers to goods trade, while participation in the single market through a Norway-style arrangement would offer much closer economic integration.

But these options come with conditions. Participation in the single market would require accepting EU rules and the free movement of people, without restoring Britain’s vote over those rules. A customs union would constrain independent trade policy and could require renegotiating trade deals signed since Brexit.

The second route is more ambitious: reopening the possibility of EU membership. Rejoining would restore British participation in EU decision-making, alongside the economic benefits of membership. But accession would require the agreement of all 27 member states, negotiations over Britain’s future obligations and some level of certainty that the next UK government wouldn’t just seek to come out again. The favourable terms the UK once enjoyed could not simply be assumed. Neither route offers a painless solution.

Burnham’s intervention nevertheless marks an important change. Where previous prime ministers largely sought to manage the consequences of Brexit while defending the settlement, he has questioned whether the settlement itself should be permanent. A decade after the referendum, British politics may be returning to its original EU dilemma.

articles.title: From aristocracy to ‘assetocracy’ – how wealth has transformed the House of Lords
articles.author: Huw Macartney, Associate professor in Political Economy, University of Birmingham
paras: On April 29, 2026, the remaining hereditary peers left the House of Lords. These 92 individuals were the last vestiges of an era in which the landed aristocracy dominated the UK’s second chamber. In the recent past, as many as 800 aristocrats filled the red benches. Now though, a new financial elite appears to have taken their place.

Gradually, the dominance of the aristocrats gave way to a more meritocratic order of life peers. In 1999, Tony Blair’s government removed most of the hereditary peers; in 2026, Keir Starmer’s government finished the job. But did removing them really make the House of Lords any less elitist?

These were some of the issues I sought to explore with a team of graduate researchers at the University of Birmingham. We set about gathering what is, to the best of our knowledge, the largest-ever repository of the financial and political activities of the Lords. Over 18 months, we collected details of all the shareholdings, company directorships, landholdings, rental properties, education, attendance and speeches in the second chamber, as well as voting records for all Lords. These are presented in my new book, The Assetocracy.

What we uncovered was staggering. More than 260 peers hold multiple, individual shareholdings – stakes in listed companies – worth more than £100,000 apiece. In fact, some Lords held more than 200 individual holdings, each valued in excess of £100,000. Even assuming each asset was only worth £100,000, that would put the combined value of those shareholdings alone at more than £22 million.

Put simply, this reflects a level of wealth far beyond that of all but the richest people in Britain. In fact, 14 Lords appear in The Sunday Times Rich List of the UK’s wealthiest people, with a combined net worth of £27.8 billion.

Moreover, half of the House are landlords with rental income. And 250 peers hold one or more paid company directorship. In short, this is an extraordinary concentration of wealth at the heart of Britain’s second chamber.

The social profile of the Lords is equally revealing. Nearly half of peers were privately educated, compared with just 7% of the wider population. Around one third went to Oxford or Cambridge, compared with just 1% nationally. And 11% attended some of Britain’s most elite schools, where annual fees can now top £60,000.

Our conclusion? The Lords is not merely wealthy, it is an institution steeped in economic, educational and social privilege. Yet remarkably little is known about the extent of this wealth. Disclosure requirements remain limited, leaving many of the peers’ financial interests hidden from public view.

And that matters. Membership of the Lords can sit alongside extremely lucrative private-sector careers. Several peers, for example, declared earning between £100,000 and £300,000 a year from company directorships and advisory positions – on top of their parliamentary roles and Lords allowances (a £371 daily rate).
Aristocrats have gone – but privilege has not

This is the paradox at the heart of the modern House of Lords. The old aristocracy may be disappearing from the red benches, but wealth and privilege have not disappeared with it. The aristocracy has increasingly given way to what we termed an “assetocracy” – members of the new financial elite whose power rests on property, finance and accumulated asset-based wealth.

Reforming the second chamber has previously been tied to either removing the aristocratic hereditary peers or (ostensibly) increasing the scope for non-elite appointments. This is primarily done through the House of Lords Appointments Commission and the introduction of crossbenchers, whose appointment does not depend on prime ministerial patronage or political donations.

Yet while these efforts appeared to be producing a diverse collection of Lords through the early 2000s, the trend was reversed with the arrival of the Conservative governments of the 2010s. Since then, my research shows that the second chamber has seen a striking influx of the new “assetocratic” elite.
Appointments of peers with shareholdings over £100,000 (by political party)

My research also reveals a small but clear relationship between wealth and participation in the Lords. Previous accounts have shown that some political donors appear to treat a peerage as a status symbol, playing little part in the day-to-day work of the House. My findings suggest however, that the pattern extends beyond political donors. On average, the wealthiest peers tend to attend less, speak less and contribute less to the work of the House.

One of the book’s central conclusions is that the rise of the assetocrats in the Lords coincided with a wider transformation of British society. It was a period when wealth inequality grew and asset ownership became an increasingly important source of economic advantage.

The Lords did not create these changes, nor are its members the only or primary beneficiaries. But my research shows how peers have often sought to narrow the terms of political debate around wealth and redistribution. They have defended a system that privileges asset ownership and particular forms of wealth accumulation.

For example, Lord Leigh of Hurley, a Conservative peer and businessman, told the House in 2025 that “we need to teach kids that so-called ‘earned income’ is paid, weekly or monthly, without any risk whatever, while ‘unearned income’ is typically generated from an investment, which involves risk to capital and, therefore, deserves greater reward”.

The research points to three conclusions. The first may seem paradoxical, but the more I researched the Lords, the more convinced I became that – certainly on issues beyond wealth and inequality – it is a remarkable source of expertise that often improves and strengthens legislation. That is why abolishing the Lords would throw away an institution that still performs an important democratic function.

Second, reform is nonetheless overdue. Prime ministerial patronage should be curtailed; minimum expectations for attendance and participation introduced; transparency over financial affairs should be increased; and outside employment more tightly regulated where it creates conflicts of interest.

But there is a bigger issue. The transformation of the Lords reflects a much more profound transformation of society. Over the past five decades, the UK has become an economy in which owning property, shares and other assets is an increasingly important route to extraordinary wealth. Removing the last vestiges of the old aristocracy from the Lords will not solve the problem. The deeper challenge is confronting the structural forces that have allowed a new asset-owning elite to take its place.

articles.title: Four ways cities can help protect democratic values
articles.author: Marta Wojciechowska, Lecturer in Politics, King's College London
paras: When people think about democracy, they tend to think about national elections, parliaments or the policies of national governments. Even the recent byelection in Holborn and St Pancras showed that democratic events are often framed around what they mean for the fortunes of national leaders, rather than what they mean for daily life within a community.

But this focus on the national level and on the procedures associated with democracy is shortsighted. Our work, bringing together political theory and local politics, is aimed at developing a deeper understanding of democracy. This is particularly important when democracies around the world are coming under threat from authoritarian leaders and insurgent populist movements.
We argue that politics at the local level, especially in cities, has a critical role to play in resisting authoritarianism. But what can cities do to promote democracy?
1. Standing up to authoritarianism
Cities have long had a strong connection to democratic values. The practices of self-governance in the city-states of ancient Greece or Renaissance Italy bore this out.

Today, cities often provide a progressive counterweight to reactionary and authoritarian politics at the national level. In the US, for example, residents in the city of Minneapolis rose up to resist deportations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials. And in India, gen-Z “cockroach” protests centred on Delhi are challenging alleged electoral fraud and government corruption.

But cities are not inherently democratic. Many elect authoritarian mayors, or enact regressive policies targeted against migrants or LGBTQ+ rights. And urban politics often fails to live up to democratic ideals by sidelining the voices of citizens and exacerbating economic inequality or feelings of social exclusion.

These dynamics can contribute to rising xenophobia and anti-democratic sentiment at the national level. So to understand why cities matter for democracy, it is important to look beyond the outcomes of elections or the agendas of individual mayors or civic movements. Instead, the deeper, more complex and often mundane ways that cities can promote democracy are what really count.
2. Challenging top-down politics

The everyday practices of governance within cities can play an important role in resisting authoritarianism and strengthening democracy. Technocratic forms of governance (that is, those that are top down and led by experts) still tend to dominate. But many cities are challenging this. They are using their legal and political autonomy to experiment with approaches that help to democratise local politics.

For example, they can give greater decision-making power to citizens by engaging them directly in policymaking at the local level. This could be through citizens’ assemblies or letting them play a role in planning the local budget. In turn, urban citizens organising themselves in communities or movements can strengthen democracy from the bottom up.
3. More economic influence for citizens

Urban economics is still generally dominated by the pursuit of growth. This can end up giving the private sector significant power over a city’s future. But some cities are experimenting with alternative approaches.

For example, community wealth building has been adopted in cities such as Cleveland, Ohio, in the US and Preston in the UK. This model promotes community-owned businesses, worker cooperatives, community banks and local control of land and real estate. By engaging citizens in economic decision-making, cities can nurture local democratic culture.
4. Providing the space to organise

Democracy is something that cuts across all aspects of urban life. This includes relations with formal institutions, such as councils. But it also takes in everyday aspects of city living, such as citizens’ relationships with the public spaces in their area.

Physical space within cities is increasingly being commercialised and privatised. But public spaces continue to be important for democratic culture. People use them to protest and put pressure on national and local governments, as happened during housing protests in cities across Spain.
The shared space of urban life can also encourage new forms of political and even moral community. These can push back against the polarisation often associated with national politics.

In an age of rising authoritarianism, urban policymakers can support democracy across multiple dimensions. Cities can certainly democratise government and economic institutions. But their most important contribution may be providing the space and support for citizens to affirm democratic values in their everyday lives.

articles.title: How we mark our ballot paper can affect how we feel about voting. Here’s why
articles.author: João V. Ferreira, Associate Professor in Economics, University of Southampton
paras: Have you ever left a polling station feeling that your mark on the ballot paper didn’t quite say what you wanted it to? Perhaps you liked two candidates but had to drop one, or backed the one who might actually win over the one you preferred.
Our feelings about democracy are important. Who wins matters, and so does whether an election feels fair. But there is another, less obvious factor: what the ballot paper allows us to say.

In his first party conference speech as prime minister, Andy Burnham announced a national commission on electoral reform and promised that Labour’s next manifesto will contain a pledge to change the voting system. Public opinion is moving his way: about 53% of voters now support a change, up from 27% in 2011.

The commission will debate whether votes should translate into seats more proportionately, and which electoral system might achieve that. But a second question deserves a place at the table: what are voters actually asked to do in the voting booth?

Putting one cross next to one name, ranking candidates or ticking every candidate you’d be happy with are very different ways of expressing political preferences. Under “pick one”, any voter who likes several candidates has no way to say so. A single cross records your first choice – not who else you would support, nor how strongly you feel.
This matters to anyone who has ever voted tactically, who felt their vote did not reflect what they think, or who stayed at home on polling day because no single option spoke for them.

The alternatives – approving multiple options or ranking candidates, for example – are known as “smarter ballots”. These deserve serious consideration in any debate on electoral reform, as they could bring both benefits and risks.

In a 2020 study I conducted with colleagues, we asked 1,977 people living in the UK to vote on COVID lockdown policies. When asked to pick just one option, only 2% were able to cast a ballot that matched their true preferences. When using a “smarter ballot” that allowed them to express more preferences, 72% were able to make a choice that corresponded to what they wanted to say.

Research on elections has yielded similar results. In field experiments in two German elections, around 2,400 voters cast their official ballot, with one vote for a candidate and one for a party. They then filled in an “approval ballot”, where they could back as many as they liked. Roughly four out of five people used that freedom to back more than one candidate or party. Today’s methods may therefore be doing a poor job of capturing what the electorate wants.

If you could better express what you think, you might feel more satisfied with your vote – in principle, at least. Yet some people appear to have a taste for simpler voting rules and to stick with what they know. The latter tendency is known as “status quo bias”.

In the German study, one voter who had backed the same party for years asked the researchers why they should change their voting behaviour. Status quo bias is particularly acute among older citizens, who are typically used to established electoral rules and may resist change.

However, smarter ballots appear to appeal to young people, as well as to politically sophisticated voters. The UK’s own history fits this pattern. The 2011 AV referendum asked UK voters whether they wanted to switch to the “alternative vote” system, where voters rank candidates in order of preference. The proposal lost heavily, but about 48% of 18 to 34-year-olds voted Yes, against 30% of those aged 35 to 65 and 19% of those older.
Ballots can change results
In 2012, in experiments across three French cities, 2,340 voters tried out smarter ballots where they could approve or grade several candidates.

France’s usual two-round system favoured “exclusive” candidates – those who are strongly liked by some voters and strongly disliked by others. The smarter ballots, however, favoured “inclusive” candidates who win broader support. In other words, the smarter ballots favoured broadly acceptable candidates, and pushed polarising ones down the list.

The German experiments point the same way. In Konstanz, the left-libertarian Pirate Party won just 4% of the official votes in the polling stations tested, but 21% of participants approved of it when using approval ballots. The Greens topped the approval vote, while the official winner, the CDU, fell to third in this alternative poll.

Transposing this on to a UK by-election, it’s possible to picture a race where Labour, the Liberal Democrats and the Greens split the vote on the centre and left. As a result, a right-leaning candidate could win with just a third of the votes. With approval ballots, the outcome could be different. Supporters could back all three of the centre and left options, and the winner might be more broadly acceptable to a larger share of the electorate.

Smarter ballots might even increase turnout: voters who feel heard may be less likely to stay at home on polling day. My experimental evidence hints at this, but it needs to be tested in real elections.

There is a real tension at play here. Rules that let voters express their views with more nuance than a single vote may run contrary to what they feel comfortable with, because some voters have a taste for simplicity and for what they already know. Tactical voting, which already exists under “pick one”, may take new forms too.
For smarter ballots to work for more than a small part of the electorate, and to overcome status quo bias, they may need to be easy to use and introduced gradually.

But the benefits for democracy could be significant: better representation of voters’ views, less polarising results, higher voter satisfaction and, potentially, higher turnout. To understand these potential benefits and risks, we need more evidence, ideally from real UK elections.

Whatever the electoral reform commission decides, it should look beyond proportional representation and ask what voters are actually being invited to say. Next time you are handed a ballot paper, ask yourself: does this piece of paper let me say what I really think?

articles.title: Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work
articles.author: Kenneth Greene, Professor of Government, The University of Texas at Austin
paras: Politics is about the distribution of power and money. So it comes as little surprise that many politicians campaign on the material benefits that citizens can expect if those candidates win.

President Donald Trump has been no different in this respect. He has promised voters, among other things, a “DOGE dividend” using money saved by cutting federal jobs, rebates from tariff revenues, and a diversion of money currently used to subsidize health insurance companies directly to Americans.

But his pledge to give US$5,000 to every U.S. citizen if Republicans retain majorities in the House and Senate in the November 2026 midterm elections had a different dimension. This offer wasn’t a rebate for taxes paid or a subsidy for an impacted constituency. Instead, it was tied to an electoral outcome. That brings it closer to vote buying, which raises concerns from a legal point of view.

For this to actually happen, it needs congressional approval – and Republican legislators haven’t taken action. But Trump has yet to rescind the idea, which could cost over $1 trillion. So it’s time to ask whether it could make a difference in the midterms, where margins are tight in key races.

I’m a political scientist who has studied for the past decade vote buying in countries around the world. Cash for votes may seem like a straightforward way to win support, but my research shows that offering people money rarely changes their vote.
Why vote buying rarely works

The practice dates back to ancient Rome and was a staple of American political machines from the 19th century to the mid-20th century in New York City, Chicago and states including Georgia, Missouri, New Jersey, Ohio and Virginia.

By diverting public money for partisan purposes, local power brokers cultivated relationships with particular constituencies, such as newly arrived immigrants. Institutional reforms, including the professionalization of government bureaucracies at the federal and local levels, slowly constricted these political machines until the last holdout in Chicago succumbed by the late 1970s.
But in recent decades, vote buying has surged in new democracies, with politicians in at least 73 countries offering cash, food, clothes, building supplies, medical care or legal advice for votes.

If vote buying is so common, it stands to reason that it must work. But a survey of recent research shows otherwise. On average, I have found that the vote-buying attempts across 10 countries and 57 elections around the world have had no detectable influence.

Why are the electoral returns so poor? For vote buying to work, the value of the benefits people receive has to outweigh the factors pushing them toward an opposing party. As in the U.S., voters around the world make their choices based on considerations such as their own partisanship; issue preferences; the performance of the incumbent party; the perceived competence of the candidates; and more. Very few voters in any electorate are truly indifferent.

As long as those factors together outweigh the value of the benefits that people would receive to switch, vote buying fails. And that’s what typically happens, as I explain in my new book, “Against the Machine.”
The importance of competition
There are three specific reasons why vote buying usually flops.

First, local competition creates vigorous campaigns that amp up partisan sentiments. These sentiments influence voters’ responses to electoral gifts. If you already like the political machine, you interpret its gifts as a sign that it cares about your welfare. But if you strongly identify with an opposing party – and therefore are a potential target of vote-buying efforts – you interpret gifts as an attempt to manipulate your vote and deprive you of basic political rights.

This calculation is one reason why vote-buying attempts can backfire, as a vivid example from Mexico shows. In 2018, two vote brokers working for Mexico’s conservative National Action Party were accosted by local voters in Nuevo Laredo. Angry residents stripped the brokers down to their underwear and painted them with the party’s blue color from head to toe, decorating them with the words “Vote for the PAN for 500 pesos.”

The second reason vote buying often fails is that competitive elections make it difficult for party machines to identify the best voters to target. Strong opposition identifiers react negatively, but weakly opposed voters might trade their vote for a payday. The trouble is that even if local vote brokers can pinpoint these voters before the election, they’re also among the most susceptible to the influence of standard campaigning. That makes them moving targets: Their changing preferences mean that machines end up inadvertently paying voters who either don’t need gifts to vote for them or would need more to actually change their decision.

Finally, even when voters who are good targets get these benefits, they often look for an escape hatch to vote their sincere preferences anyway. The secret ballot provides one if they trust that it’s truly secret.

It turns out that people are acutely aware of who’s watching them vote. When they see poll watchers only from the party machine, they worry that their votes could be discovered by spies, cameras or by other means. But when they also see poll watchers from an opposing party, they believe that ballot secrecy is preserved and that they can vote sincerely without punishment.

Taken together, these reasons have led me to optimistically conclude that the effectiveness of vote buying depends not on the party machine’s prowess but on the strength of the parties that oppose it.
Vote buying has a checkered recent history in elections around the world, but could the “Trump dividend” swing the midterms? I see that scenario as unlikely.

Partisanship, a core element that makes people resistant to vote buying, is very strong in the U.S. electorate. There’s no need to pay committed Republicans, while committed Democrats will see the offer as a bald monetization of politics that can deepen their antagonism.
The design of Trump’s offer also makes it likely to flounder. Promising to pay everyone gets around the targeting challenge, but it also creates what social scientists call a “free-rider problem.”

At issue is that people tend to behave in selfish ways. If they expect a certain outcome anyway, they’ll make a decision based on self-interest. For example, independents and less committed Democrats who could be swayed by a $5,000 check might think they can avoid feeling like a sellout if they vote sincerely but they will still get paid as long as others switch their vote to Republican.

In theory, there is one way Trump’s offer could succeed. Research shows that buying turnout, rather than trying to change vote choices, is routinely effective. But all the examples come from countries where party officials actively monitor who comes to the polls. Without that surveillance, which is illegal in the U.S., the free-rider problem could bedevil turnout as well.

But whether enacted or not, the promise of cash for votes has a big downside for democracy. It means that no one will know whether victorious Republican candidates won this November because Americans preferred their policies and gave them a mandate – or because they expected to get paid.
Kenneth Greene's research has been funded by the National Science Foundation, the University of Texas at Austin, and the Mellon Foundation.

articles.title: Why the political ambition gap between men and women persists even at the local level
articles.author: Emma Schroeder, Assistant Professor of Political Science, Texas Christian University
paras: An appointment to a local library commission, reluctantly accepted, may not sound like an auspicious event. For Nancy Pelosi, however, that 1973 appointment launched what would become one of the most influential careers in modern American politics.

Pelosi’s work on the commission led to opportunities for higher office until she eventually reached her position as the first woman to serve as speaker of the House in 2007, shaping politics and policy in the United States for a generation.

Leading up to the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, the public’s attention is on national races. But like Pelosi, many of the women who have been elected to Congress launched their careers at the local level: Ayanna Pressley, Tammy Baldwin, Sarah Palin and Mia Love, to name a few.
For these women, local office served as an entry point to higher office. Yet their experiences raise an important question: How likely are women to be ambitious for local office in the first place?
Political scientists define political ambition as an individual’s interest in or intention to run for elected office.

Scholars know that women are less likely than men to be interested in pursuing state and national political office. In our recently conducted analysis, Gender and Local Political Ambition, published in the Elements in Gender and Politics series from Cambridge University Press, we investigate whether the gap in ambition for office persists locally. Along with co-authors Christina Wolbrecht, Mirya Holman and Lakshmi Iyer, we surveyed 2,000 civically and politically engaged Americans to understand how women view local offices, their motivations for seeking them and whether they are just as ambitious for them as men.
We found that the gender gap endures and women remain less ambitious for local office compared to men. However, the women who do express ambition tend to be ambitious for local office only.
Local office: Closer to home, closer to issues
For women, local politics may present a best-case scenario for those interested in seeking office.

The positions are closer to home, making it easier for officeholders to balance the demands of public service and their personal lives. Running for local offices also requires less time and money to mount successful campaigns. For women, who often find campaigning more challenging, this is especially attractive.

Though harassment, threats and violence toward women still occur in local contexts, the lower visibility of being a local government official rather than holding a state or federal office means this violence may occur less frequently.

Local government may also provide a setting uniquely suited for women to engage in problem solving, as the opportunity to work toward resolving problems in their own communities may be more attractive to them.
Lower confidence, not lower qualifications
While local office might be more attractive to women, the ambition gender gap persists.

We found that women’s lesser ambition can be attributed to lower confidence in their ability to serve. They view themselves as underqualified, though on paper they are often overqualified. Women also receive less encouragement to pursue local office from their family and community networks.

The women we surveyed were especially concerned about harassment and violence, with good reason. Women holding local office across the country report increasing levels of harassment and threats, such as Emma Mulvaney-Stanak, the mayor of Burlington, Vermont, who was subjected to stalking this year.
Given our sample of highly engaged Americans, these are the women we might expect to be most interested in attaining local office. Yet they are still less ambitious than men.
Women, men seek office for different reasons
Even women who are politically ambitious are more likely to seek only local-level office rather than state or federal office.
Women in our surveys expressed a strong desire to seek local office to make a difference and solve problems within their community.

One respondent wanted to improve the “quality of life and access to services for (her) community.” Another noted that she wanted to use her education and experience to “add to the conversation and be part of the solution rather than the bitchfest.”

For the women in our sample, the needs of their immediate community were a source of motivation. Specifically, women cited as motivators “affordable housing,” “crime” and “poverty,” and in some cases “corruption.” One respondent put it bluntly, saying, “Our city leaders are rather useless. They make poor decisions and don’t strive to represent their constituents.”

Women were also less likely to aspire to higher office, perhaps because local office provides the ideal venue to solve the problems they care about most. By contrast, men tended to view local office primarily as a pathway to higher office.
Local gender gap varies by race, ethnicity, LGBTQ+ identity

Differences also emerged across identity groups. Black women were especially likely to concentrate their ambitions at the local level, while Hispanic women were more likely to look beyond local office.

We found that LGB-identifying respondents were not particularly ambitious for local, state or federal office, whereas trans and nonbinary people were more ambitious for local compared to higher office.
There is no shortage of skilled and qualified women to run for local office. Ambition is partially to blame for their underrepresentation in those offices.
Our research offers insight on closing this gap, such as encouraging women to run for local office and encouraging local organizations to recruit women for candidate training programs.

The next generation of women politicians could just be waiting for one person to encourage them to seek local office. As more women serve in local offices, they may inspire other women to follow in their paths, helping develop the next generation of political leaders.

The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: The new battleground: the UK’s disinformation centre faces threats on multiple fronts
articles.author: Paul Baines, Professor of Political Marketing, Head of Executive Education, University of Leicester
paras: Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently announced the creation of a National Centre for Information Defence that will disrupt disinformation campaigns by states hostile to the UK. The centre will bring together security services, police, tech firms and government departments.

But this new centre will have its work cut out. State-backed adversaries are supported by huge amounts of money – Russia alone has an estimated US$2.15 billion (£1.63 billion) annual budget for information manipulation. And China spends more, at an estimated US$10 billion (£7.6 billion). This is alongside AI-generated deepfakes and covert digital operations.

Russia, China and Iran are mounting simultaneous operations to try to destabilise democratic governments. The UK’s new agency will have to bridge government departments and partner with and temper big tech in order to respond effectively.
In a recent podcast interview, Burnham said there had been clear Russian interference in the UK’s 2016 Brexit referendum. He later made a similar claim in the Commons.

Charges of Russian interference in elections around the world are nothing new. After the 2016 US presidential election, the Mueller Report concluded that Russia interfered in the 2016 US presidential election in a “sweeping and systematic fashion”.

And the UK’s Intelligence and Security Committee criticised the government for failing to properly investigate Russian interference in British politics. However, before Burnham’s podcast interview, the UK government had not confirmed Russian interference in the Brexit referendum, despite allegations circulating in the media.

More broadly, the level of disinformation attacks aimed at the UK is worrying. The head of MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, said that the UK is dealing with more threats from other states than during the cold war. He added that Russia was “aggressor number one” (but later clarified that Russia had not succeeded in influencing the Brexit referendum result).

Disinformation itself is as old as the hills – trickery is a fundamental instrument of geopolitical conflict. Election interference is also not new. But in the AI era, disinformation operates with unprecedented speed, precision and creativity. Modern disinformation misleads and spreads harm, operating in the shadows, and is specifically designed to fall beneath the threshold for war.

The rationale is simple: why bother lobbing weapons if you can destroy an adversary’s morale? A hostile state will spend more on disinformation if it means spending less on costlier conventional weapon systems. And states are less likely to be held accountable for any damage they cause.
The primary threats to UK democracy come from Russia, China and Iran – and to a lesser extent from North Korea.

Russia relies on a strategy called “reflexive control”. This involves trying to manipulate citizens in target countries into certain behaviour – such as voting in a way that benefits Russia. It seeks to paralyse political decision-making and fracture alliances, including Nato and the EU.

China approaches information conflict through its “three warfares strategy”. This refers to psychological, public opinion and legal domains. It could include attempts to shape narratives around China’s policies on trade, Taiwan or the origins of COVID; or it might use digital deception and intimidation to win support in disputes over borders or control of the South China Sea. The aim is to break resistance without fighting.

Meanwhile, Iran invests heavily in cyber-influence operations. It has sought to stoke dissent over Scottish independence, access and leak information on Iranian dissident journalists and attack infrastructure such as power plants. In this way, Iran could undermine regional stability, radicalise target groups and manipulate public debate.

North Korea uses similar tactics, but for espionage, disruption and theft. One example is believed to be the WannaCry ransomware attack in 2017, which disrupted 61 NHS organisations including hospitals.

The UK’s main adversaries target the democratic process itself. They view democratic institutions, election campaigns and referendums as a country’s “centre of gravity”. As such, disrupting elections threatens the very stability of a democratic country.

The UK’s vulnerability was laid bare in a 2021 report by the Intelligence and Security Committee (ISC). The report revealed that Russian interference in British politics was widespread. Social media manipulation, illicit financial flows and cyber-operations were listed as tactics.

The report concluded that the UK had seriously underestimated the Russian threat. Notably, the intelligence services were accused of not investigating credible allegations of foreign interference during the 2014 Scottish independence referendum and the 2016 Brexit vote. This reluctance to scrutinise foreign interference had created a space for hostile adversaries to exploit.

Since the UK showed support for Ukraine, the threat has worsened. Former national security adviser Lord Ricketts recently warned that the UK faces the threat of cyber-attacks on its banking systems, energy or water supplies as the Kremlin seeks to undermine public support for Ukraine.

The new Centre for Information Defence has to do more than just rebut disinformation. It also needs to expose target audiences to common manipulation tactics and deepfake media. Archetypes like Project Servator and See It, Say It, Sorted point the way to communicating this type of threat to the public.

Beyond public awareness, resilience requires stronger media ecosystems and digital platforms. Social media companies need to enforce stricter rules over algorithms and quicker removal of fake accounts.

Sanctions against individual perpetrators could include naming and shaming, freezing assets or travel bans. The 2023 National Security Act criminalised covert foreign interference, but the legislation needs to be enforced more robustly. Fines could encourage digital platforms to comply, but governments must also do more to freeze hostile states out of diplomatic relations. They could also coordinate condemnation through alliances such as Nato, the EU and the G7.

Given the rapid evolution of AI and the blurring of boundaries between peace and war, a hesitant response is not enough. But to tackle the huge threat, the new centre needs to be well resourced – in funding, capability, human resources and leeway. Crucially, it should also focus on offence as well as defence. Boxers don’t simply parry opponents’ punches – they must land their own too.
Paul Baines is a Conservative Councillor at Charnwood Borough Council and Deputy Leader of the Charnwood Conservative Group.

articles.title: COVID inquiry: four ways to improve support for people with intellectual disabilities
articles.author: Richard Hastings, 125th Anniversary Chair, and Professor of Psychology Health and Social Care, University of Birmingham
paras: Anxiety. I always feel like I’m on edge. COVID, cost of living crisis, finances, current living arrangement. The majority don’t seem to care about COVID anymore and you can’t just ignore it, people are still dying from it.

Cara, whose name has been changed, described these concerns in our research into the continuing effects of the pandemic on people with intellectual disabilities. Her account shows how concerns about infection became entangled with uncertainty about everyday life.

The UK COVID-19 Inquiry’s care sector report, published on October 20 2026, focuses on how to improve support before another emergency. For people with intellectual disabilities, known as learning disabilities in the UK, that requires attention to how people live and the different kinds of support they need and receive.

The report’s first recommendation calls for pandemic planning at government, local and provider levels. But the formal recommendations are framed mainly in relation to care homes for older people and leave important details unspecified about how those plans should meet the needs of people with intellectual disabilities.

Our expert report to the inquiry, developed with input from people with intellectual disabilities and families, proposed more explicit commitments. These provide a starting point for addressing those gaps.
Protecting support for everyday life

People with intellectual disabilities have varied support needs. Our expert report describes most provision extends beyond residential care, including support for people living with family or in their own homes. Planning must also consider the services that help people participate in their communities.

Our study following adults through the pandemic found that access to day services had not returned to pre-pandemic levels by late 2022. Among adults interviewed directly, 37% had reported regularly attending before the pandemic; 26% were using some form of day service in the final research round.
These figures indicate why lifting restrictions did not necessarily restore people’s opportunities.
In our in-depth interviews, participants described losing independence and activities that were important to them. Future planning needs to address those consequences alongside infection control.

The inquiry’s first recommendation does not explicitly require protection of day services or community participation. In our expert report, we recommended planning to increase support during emergencies, while protecting access to community activities. Governments should explain how their response will achieve this.
Making health protection accessible
Public health advice is useful only if people can understand it and act on it.

Our expert recommendations called for information suitable for people with intellectual disabilities to be available at the same time as information for the general public. We also recommended prioritising the social care support people need to access healthcare, including vaccination.

The inquiry’s third recommendation requires accessible information about financial support schemes for care workers and providers. Its formal recommendations do not make an equivalent, explicit commitment to timely, accessible public health information for people with intellectual disabilities and their families.

Governments should build that requirement into pandemic plans. People with intellectual disabilities should help develop and test guidance before an emergency, with arrangements for updating it as advice changes.

Plans should also explain how people will receive practical help to follow that guidance or attend healthcare appointments. Publishing accessible advice cannot, by itself, resolve the loss of someone’s usual support.
Recognising intensive support needs

Families of people with profound and multiple intellectual disabilities described particularly difficult experiences in our research into their lives during the pandemic. They reported difficulties obtaining healthcare and support, alongside exhaustion and anxiety about the future.

The inquiry documents the loss of respite care and its consequences for unpaid carers. Yet its eight formal recommendations contain no dedicated requirement to maintain respite or other support for unpaid carers, or provide replacement care if a family carer becomes ill.

For people with profound and multiple intellectual disabilities, replacement support must be appropriate to their individual needs. Emergency arrangements should explain how someone’s care will continue if the people who usually support them become unavailable.

Our expert report recommended prioritising these individuals and their carers. Governments should make that priority explicit when implementing the inquiry’s planning recommendation, with resources to sustain support.
Including people outside existing services
Another gap concerns adults with intellectual disabilities who do not qualify for social care.

Our expert report called for better understanding of their lives and how their needs might increase during an emergency. Planning around existing social care recipients alone risks missing this large group.
Councils should work with people with intellectual disabilities and local organisations to establish accessible ways to seek help when circumstances change.
The How We Survive and Thrive commission, organised by Learning Disability England, has developed similar recommendations about maintaining support and involving people in decisions.

As governments implement the inquiry’s findings, people with intellectual disabilities and their families should help judge whether the resulting plans address their needs. Those plans must explain how support will remain available across different living arrangements, including for people who were managing without formal services before an emergency began.

articles.title: US inequality is getting worse in ways you might not expect
articles.author: Markus Schneider, Associate Professor of Economics, University of Denver
paras: The buzzword of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections may be affordability, but growing anger over inequality is behind the sentiment.

A Pew Research survey released in October 2026 found that roughly 6 in 10 Americans – including 4 in 10 Republicans – believe there’s too much inequality in the U.S. And a growing share from both major political parties state that the economy needs to be fundamentally rebuilt to address this.

This sentiment has, however, been difficult to convert into political results. Public support for California’s proposed wealth tax on billionaires has been waning ahead of the midterms, for example, and in 2025, Republicans passed President Donald Trump’s sweeping legislation that included tax cuts for the wealthy while cutting safety net programs.

I’m an economist who has been studying inequality for about two decades. My research confirms the trend of rising inequality since 1980, driven by the wealthiest pulling away not just from the middle class, but also from the “merely wealthy.” Overall, recent research underscores how policy choices – including taxation and public spending – enabled this 40-year rise in inequality.

Some policies enacted more recently appear to be accelerating this trend. An analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%.

Recent federal data shows that wealth inequality continues to grow. The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion. That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 – and from 27.4% in 1999.

These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class – the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% – who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group that’s 40 times larger than the top 1%. And the middle’s share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data.

But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows. This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth – almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%. Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026.
Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories.

Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is disproportionately boosted by corporate profits, which are up sharply overall. The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfolios’ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability that’s driving up stock prices – especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom.
Since President Ronald Reagan’s tax cuts in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become less and less progressive, often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats.

The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research – including international studies – doesn’t back that up. A 2025 Brookings report notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth.

Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trump’s sweeping policy and tax bill, which included provisions making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent. Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the lowest corporate tax rate since 1940.

It’s also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because the composition of their wealth is different. They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from.

Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%’s wealth portfolio consists of corporate and business ownership, allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways – including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability. Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can borrow against it for cash, usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares.

By contrast, below that elite, real estate is a much more important component of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share. For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%.
The new drivers of inequality

Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played. But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed.

One example is a provision in Trump’s 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse. Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by about 5 million due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs.

The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point. They disproportionately affect low- and middle-income consumers but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy – while boosting the profits of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil. This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which has pushed up the global price of oil.

Then there are tariffs, which are fundamentally a consumption tax on imports. Economists at the New York Federal Reserve have found that these levies have inflicted a heavy hit on many common consumer goods. They estimated that prices for these items, which make up a much larger share of household budgets among the nonwealthy, would have fallen on average by 1% over the year without the tariffs. Instead, they have risen by 2.9%.

This acceleration in the redistribution of wealth from the middle class to the very top, in short, has an array of drivers. But they’re not inexorable forces of history. As economist Thomas Piketty put it in “A Brief History of Equality,” published in 2022: “Inequality is first of all a social, historical, and political construction.”

Markus Schneider does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: How governments worldwide are shaping what AI can say about politics
articles.author: Jordi Calvet-Bademunt, Research Fellow and Visiting Scholar of Political Science, Vanderbilt University
paras: With the U.S. midterms approaching, about 1 in 5 voters has asked AI chatbots about elections and politics, a recent survey found.

But many voters may not know that governments around the world increasingly shape what chatbots can say. And because many tech companies apply the same policies worldwide, the answers American voters get may be shaped by governments at home and abroad.

I’m a researcher at a nonpartisan think tank at Vanderbilt University, where I study free speech policy. In two reports published in 2025 and 2026, my colleagues and I worked with global legal experts to examine how governments in 12 countries and regions regulate artificial intelligence. Our research shows that they often use existing rules, such as national security or anti-state propaganda laws, rather than new AI laws to control what AI models can say.
Censorship masked as safety
AI can cause real harm, from launching cyberattacks to generating sexualized images of children.

It’s important that governments tackle these harms. But, in our assessment, some governments use legitimate concerns like these as a pretext to control political discussion, particularly chatbot responses about those in power.

In 2024, an Indian journalist asked Google’s Gemini chatbot whether the policies of India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, were fascist. Gemini responded that some experts say yes. The government reacted by requiring official permission before “unreliable” AI models could be released. Although authorities later dropped this requirement, the case shows how terms like “under-testing” or “unreliable” can be used for political purposes.
India is not alone. China requires AI models to uphold “socialist core values.”

And in Turkey, a court blocked posts by Grok, the chatbot built into the social platform X, that allegedly insulted President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, founding father Mustafa Kemal Atatürk and religious values. Research by Turkish law scholar Yaman Akdeniz identifies the Turkish rulings as among the earliest documented cases of state censorship of chatbots.

Vietnam shows what such content controls can mean for dissidents, including those in exile. A Vietnamese court sentenced two activists, who live in Germany, to 17 years each in prison in December 2025 for spreading anti-state material. Prosecutors accused them of using AI to fake voices and images of Vietnamese leaders, illustrating how prosecutions can target political criticism.
Foreign rules, domestic impact
Some of these government measures only affect people residing in their countries. Other statutes cross borders.

The European Union’s AI Act, adopted in 2024, requires any company offering AI tools in Europe, wherever it is based, to mark AI-generated content. Anthropic, for one, applies the marks globally because it has no reliable way to apply them by region. This is an example of the Brussels Effect, in which rules adopted in the EU end up applying elsewhere.
European rules also affect what chatbots say about politics.

In August 2026, the EU placed ChatGPT under the strictest tier of its Digital Services Act, Europe’s online safety rulebook. OpenAI, creator of ChatGPT, now must assess and reduce the “systemic risks” of its service, including risks to elections, such as the spread of disinformation.

And the Dutch Data Protection Authority tested four chatbots before the 2025 national election and found that the political middle ground “virtually disappears” in their voting advice. It urged providers to “prevent their systems from being used for voting advice.”
These rules can be used to pressure platforms.

In 2024, Thierry Breton, then the EU’s top digital rules enforcer, reminded Elon Musk of his legal obligations before Musk’s live interview with then-presidential candidate Donald Trump on X, warning against the spread of “harmful content.”
The United States is no exception
Threats to Americans’ access to information do not come only from abroad.

In 2025, President Trump issued an executive order on “Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government.” It requires the AI models the government buys to be “truth-seeking,” ideologically neutral and not favoring ideas such as “diversity, equity and inclusion.”

“Truth-seeking” may sound like an objective, neutral term, but it can mean very different things to different people. Take media reporting: The president recently banned three news outlets from the White House for reporting “FICTION and LIES” and dismissed media polls as “fake.”
More recently, the Federal Trade Commission has suggested that AI companies that steer answers toward undisclosed ideological or biased objectives might break consumer protection law.

A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 8 in 10 Americans believe Republican and Democratic voters cannot agree on basic facts. In other words, as our report notes, government mandates to seek truth are often driven by ideological belief systems, particularly on political issues.

Meanwhile, dozens of states have passed laws restricting AI-generated political deepfakes. California and Hawaii, for example, are two states that have banned sharing deceptive AI content about candidates in the months around an election. U.S. courts have blocked both of those laws, citing the First Amendment.

What does this mean for voters? When you ask your chatbot about the elections, treat the answer as a starting point. Keep in mind that governments, both foreign and domestic, may try to influence the answer. AI responses should not replace your critical thinking at the ballot box.

Jordi Calvet-Bademunt is affiliated with The Future of Free Speech, a nonpartisan, nonprofit think tank located at Vanderbilt University. The organization is supported by foundations and individual donors, and it retains full independence and final authority over its work, including research, methodology, analysis, conclusions, and presentation.

articles.title: Are partisan politics even changing up our accents? They just might be, y’all
articles.author: Valerie M. Fridland, Professor of Linguistics, University of Nevada, Reno
paras: With the midterms fast approaching, communicating just the right message has been top of mind on all sides of the political aisle.

Whether that message drives home a lack of affordability as gas, food and home prices surge or stokes fears about the rise of communism in the American heartland, Democrats and Republicans are spending a lot of time thinking about what to say.

But as a linguist who studies the impact of accents on the way people are perceived, I believe how politicians and voters say what they say might be just as important as the words they use in understanding the social consequences and linguistic changes resulting from the political divides that are growing between us.

If there is one regional American accent that has long endured on the lips of its speakers – as well as in the minds of listeners beyond the region – it’s the Southern accent. From North Carolina through Texas and pretty much all states in between, the so-called Southern drawl has long been emblematic of a distinct culture found in the South.

Yet, in the urban South, recent linguistic research finds that the drawl’s most salient features are starting to fade on the lips of young speakers. Fewer “pins” are merged with “pens,” and pronunciations such as “far” for “fire” or “say-ud” for “said” are becoming rarer.

While linguists have been busy trying to understand this trend, political scientists have been measuring how different accents perform on the campaign trail. The verdict? Southern accented candidates are generally heard as more conservative than those without a Southern accent, particularly to Democratic listeners.

Putting these findings from linguists and political scientists together, alongside a spate of studies examining correlations between voting patterns and vowels, hints, I believe, that the increasing conservative-liberal divide in American politics just might be the key to understanding what’s driving the decline of the drawl in the urban South.
Out of the mouth of the South

The traditional Southern accent has no shortage of stereotypes: From positive, friendly, country and down-home vibes to negative, backward, uneducated and lazy tropes, the accents of William Faulkner, Bill Clinton and the hillbilly Clampetts have weathered it all.
The reality, of course, is that the Southern accent is not some incorrect version of a national standard but instead a historically separate and unique dialect – or, more accurately, set of dialects.

As explored in my recent book, this dialect formed from linguistic variation that came in with colonial-era settlers from different places and stations. The incipient differences increased after the Civil War intensified hostilities and cultural differences between the North and South.

The association with “countryness” often triggered by a Southern accent grew out of this region’s agricultural past and its related cultural folkways. But what “country” has come to mean relies largely on stereotypes about what a country lifestyle involves. They include things like hunting, gun ownership and less socially progressive views – often arising from media portrayals of and beliefs about the South.

As the South has become more and more industrialized over the past half-century, these social meanings associated with the accent’s use now highlight a disconnect between its new urban vibe and its older, traditional rural one.
As rural vs. urban ideological and political divides in the U.S. have intensified, so has using symbolic means to signal this opposition.

Pickup trucks emblazoned with American flags and country music have become politicized. The white Southern accent, by virtue of its association with more rural traditional values, has also become emblematic of a conservative political identity not all modern Southerners share.

Recent linguistic research has compared voters in the South who had strong Southern accents to those with weaker ones, mainly measured through their use of a set of unique Southern vowel pronunciations, such as saying “bay-ud” for “bed” or “rawed” for “ride.”

It turns out that those holding more right-leaning positions and voting Republican in previous presidential elections used significantly more Southern vowels than those with more left-leaning positions who voted for Democrats. Three separate studies in Georgia, North Carolina and Tennessee discovered the same relationship between degree of Southern accent and political conservatism or liberalism.
The takeaway from these studies is that conservatism itself is embodied in a strong Southern accent.
New sound to the urban South?
The pronunciation of one’s vowels has become a barometer of how one’s beliefs and values fit within the old vs. new South.

Conservative ideologies and politics have become enmeshed with “country” speech and lifestyles. Young urban Southerners who don’t identify with these traits might be moving not so much away from Southern identity itself but rather specifically from this rural conservative identity it is often associated with.

Of course, other factors are also playing a role in the decline of the Southern accent in cities, such as heavy migration by non-Southerners to the region and greater interaction with people from other dialect areas via social media.

Outside the South, interestingly, recent research has found a greater embrace of Southern accent features, emerging in particular among those in rural areas where traditional lifestyles and, often, more conservative views are embraced. For instance, in a small, rural town in Ohio, speakers who identified themselves as more drawn to country lifestyles showed use of vowel features – such as saying “baa” for “bye” – more associated with the South.

So, in this circuitous and indirect way, vowels have become the latest players in partisan politics: Democratic Southerners wanting to distance themselves from the ideological and political climate associated with the rural South are moving away from its unique vowels. More “traditional” or conservative-leaning speakers continue to embrace them.

The real casualty in this particular battleground might be the obscuring of a larger culture, practice and community that the Southern accent has long represented for those who are automatically – and often erroneously – assigned a politicized identity just by the sound of their voice.
